create-edit.title: Streamlining CRM data property management experiences

intro.p1: Solving customer pains, driving adoption, and reducing overhead costs by rethinking a core data management workflow in HubSpot's CRM.

context.title: Context.
context.//p1: HubSpot is an extremely robust application that includes multiple products to provide a really wide-ranging offering for marketers. The CRM sits at the core of their product offering and it’s where customers first set up the infrastructure of their HubSpot experience. With such a robust application comes robust growth, and with robust growth comes robust debt. Falling into that category was the Data Infra/Data Management part of the application that either gets visited in the beginning of a customer’s experience or not until they have a need for those tools later down the road.
context.//p2: Ten-plus years into development, there were more tools and features available than most customers would ever deal with. On top of this, when you factor in portal type, ie., SMB, enterprise, etc, this makes the offering even more complex. This was no different when it came to creating and managing custom data properties. The workflow [as it existed] was built in a wizard framework with limited flexibility to improve velocity. It also included a limited means to deliver feedback during the process which added confusion and friction while trying to both create or manage a unique property.
context.p1: HubSpot's CRM sits at the core of their product offering and it’s where customers first set up the infrastructure of their HubSpot experience. To make that good first impression, our goal was to have a best-in-class onboarding data onboarding and integration experience.
context.p2: The challenge with this particular workflow was trying to offer a robust data creation and management experience for customers of all sizes while still making it feel nimble. Based on internal and external sentiment, the current framework for creating and managing data properties was rigid, redundant, and limited; basically the antithesis of the original goal.

opportunity.title: Opportunity.
opportunity.//p1: Between the customer support contact volume related to managing properties, some new features we were preparing for internally, and an opportunity to start formally preparing for and adopting some new design standards our core team was working on, we seized on the moment to prioritize exploring and delivering a new core workflow for creating and managing properties.
opportunity.p1: We had enough of a backlog to inform us that customer support was swamped and customers were clearly frustrated with both existing and new features in the workflow. The problem was that this was a serious commitment with potential to not move the needle as much as some other projects we had in our pipeline. With that in mind, our pitch centered on four key goals:

1.goal: Reduce redundancy by exploring a less rigid flow
1.result: New flow doesn’t require redundant actions and is not strictly linear

2.goal: Reduce relevant support volume by a meaningful amount
2.result: Support volume reduced by ~35% WoW (~20% expected)

3.goal: Improve visibility of new property types and additions
3.result: New test and released property types saw nearly doubled adoption rate in first week compared to previous rate

4.goal: Improve UX flexibility for AI and KB helpers to help drive usage of them
4.result: New framework includes content slots for AI/ML and KB inclusions to keep customers on task and doesn’t drive them away

creation.title: Redundant, rigid, and in need of replacement.
creation.//p1: One of the biggest issues with creating properties was the customer’s desire to test properties and verify feasibility before committing to a specific property. This problem skewed more towards the more advanced property types, but even for simple text properties there was a desire to see if what they wanted made sense and was actually doable.

The workflow only really functioned in one direction. The unfortunate part of that decision was if you wanted to change a detail about the property, you would lose all progress that you had made. Even a simple thing like changing the property name required up to three clicks to get back to the details stage.
creation.p1: Even with a robust backlog, I wanted to get a better picture of customer pain by meeting with a cohort of beta customers. After a dozen or so conversations, the same themes kept coming up: the workflow is rigid and doesn't let them accomplish things in one shot, there are too many required hoops even to set up a simple property, and it doesn't drive adoption of new updates that are useful to them.
creation.//p2: With the linear wizard format, that meant jumping through some hoops just to get to the more “playground” aspect and caused a lot of friction for customers.
creation.p2: If a customer had to make even the slightest change, their expectation was to at least persist the information they had already entered.
creation.p3: Going back meant needing to go all the way back. This problem in itself almost became a battle cry based on the number of times it was shared in feedback.
creation.//p3: Then, at the same time, if a customer wanted to go back, that meant losing all of their work because it wouldn’t translated across properties (this had technical limitations in many cases, but for common cases it could be solved).
creation.p4: Sadly, this was even more painful for more complex property types where maybe a customer had spent several minutes trying to create and test a custom formula.
creation.//p4: Going back meant needing to go all the way back. This became a regular headache for most customers.
creation.//p5: By changing the flow to be non-linear and more of a CYOA experience, we could improve upon several things related to this problem.
creation.p5: The management flow was not so far different, but located in a different panel. Even with a change of space, the primary issue for management revolved around scalability and data density.

manage.title: Fixing friction with unity.
manage.//p1: After creating a property there are some actions that some more admin-type customers may want to take, but its not immediately apparent how/where they can take them. On top of that, certain messaging and feedback was limited in how it was being presented because of the small panel that the properties existed in. That same issue also existed for modifying a property like a dropdown/select and trying to test a formula; all were either not doable or difficult to do in the space that customers had to try in.
manage.p1: Creating and managing properties are, for the most part, admin tasks that have a need for efficiency. In talking to our beta customers, the top three terms that they conveyed for any new features were, "make it efficient," "make it flexible," and "make it familiar."
manage.p2: Therefore, my primary objective was to strategize and craft toward a more unified experience with minimal trade-offs in current and future-looking functionality.
manage.//p2: There were other issues at play related to managing properties that fell out of scope for this project (things like core actions, ie, deleting, copying, etc), but by migrating the management experience to the same framework as the new creation experience, it allowed for more flexibility to perform a task and also allowed for more visibility and discovery for problem-solving tasks. It also allowed for down-the-road improvements like integrations, AI/ML augments, and KB helper injection so that customers would gain more clarity in the moment as opposed to being shepherded away for most of those moments.
manage.p3: The old panel left a lot to be desired according to internal and external anecdotes. It was also starting to get crowded with information and began to feel cramped. With more content and features on the way, it needed to change so that it could scale.
manage.p4: The updated experience allowed for more of the free-flow of information and flexibility that our admin customers were craving for some time.

retro.title: Next steps and reflections.
retro.p1: The delivered experiences were meeting their intended goals as of spring 2024 when we released both apps into beta. We met with and surveyed customers in a closed beta before getting a quick confidence boost from our support team that their volume didn’t increase (closed beta group was too small to measure a significant change WoW, so we only had them focus on targeted feedback from that group). With that, we posted our public beta and received several dozen adoptions in the first couple of days. From there, it grew to over 300 by the end of the following week, and eventually reached about  15% of the customer base in Pro+ tier very soon after that. Our CSAT remained at ~75%+ from initial release day (peaked around 86% at one point) and customer support reported volume on certain topics related to management and creation started to decrease exponentially until we hit our first 20% WoW reduction goal around day 23 of public beta.
retro.p2: At the same time, there were two UX projects happening concurrently while engineering was in the middle of rebuilding the core tech stack for this product area: this framework delivery for creation and management and an encapsulated quick property creation experience for use outside of the admin space. The quick property creation project actually spawned the larger project, funny enough.
retro.p3: The coalescing projects meant that a lot of planning was needed to deliver properly. One thing I would reflect on for this projects relates to communication. At one point I was on one track of work and unaware of what my engineering partners were working on. We discovered that we were working on opposite projects at one point and that syncing back up to get back on track was going to take at least a week. This all could’ve been alleviated by a one-line clarification in a Slack message. It taught me a lesson about properly setting the table and making sure that each partner in the pod is aligned at the right time.
